title: CAR T-Cell Therapy Puts Severe Rheumatoid Arthritis Into Remission in Landmark First Trial
excerpt: Three of six patients achieved sustained medication-free remission after a single infusion in the world's first CAR T-cell trial for rheumatoid arthritis
body:
• Three of six patients with severe, treatment-resistant rheumatoid arthritis achieved sustained medication-free remission after a single CAR T-cell infusion in the world's first trial of its kind
  • The therapy, mivocabtagene autoleucel (miv-cel), tracked and eliminated disease-driving B cells deep within joints, bone marrow and lymph nodes, producing a greater than 90% median reduction in autoantibodies
  • A phase 2 trial with 10 additional patients is now underway at Charité Berlin to compare CAR T-cell therapy against existing B-cell-targeting drugs

A single infusion of genetically modified immune cells has put half the patients in a small but landmark clinical trial into sustained remission from severe rheumatoid arthritis, according to results published August 27 in Nature Medicine.

The COMPARE trial, conducted at Charité–Universitätsmedizin Berlin, is the first clinical study to test a CD19-directed CAR T-cell therapy in rheumatoid arthritis. All six patients enrolled — three women and three men aged 31 to 69 — had exhausted up to eight biologic and targeted therapies over a decade without adequate relief.

How CAR T-Cell Therapy Works Against Autoimmune Disease

CAR T-cell therapy was originally developed for blood cancers. The approach involves extracting a patient's own T cells, engineering them in a laboratory to carry a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) that recognizes the CD19 molecule on B cells, and infusing them back after a short course of preparatory chemotherapy.

In autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis, certain B cells — memory cells of the adaptive immune system — persist in joints, bone marrow and lymph nodes, producing harmful autoantibodies that drive chronic inflammation. The engineered CAR T cells seek out and destroy these disease-driving B cells wherever they hide, effectively resetting the immune system.

"Disease activity decreased markedly in all six patients. During follow-up of up to one year, three patients were in sustained remission without any medication for rheumatoid arthritis. This is particularly remarkable given that none of the established treatments had previously been able to relieve their symptoms adequately."

— Prof. Gerhard Krönke, Charité and German Rheumatology Research Center

Trial Results Show Immune Reset

The therapy, mivocabtagene autoleucel (miv-cel) developed by Kyverna Therapeutics, demonstrated rapid CAR T-cell expansion in the blood, peaking within three weeks. B cells were profoundly depleted not only in peripheral blood but also in deeper tissue compartments, confirmed through synovial and bone marrow biopsies.

All six patients showed decreased disease activity, with a median 49% reduction in DAS28-CRP scores. Five patients achieved ACR20 responses, four reached ACR50, and two met ACR70 criteria. Autoantibody levels dropped by more than 90% in median, with sustained seroconversion to normal ACPA and rheumatoid factor levels achieved in most patients.

Critically, when B cells eventually repopulated, they were predominantly naïve cells that had not been shaped by the disease. The disease-driving B cells present before treatment were no longer detectable in almost all patients. Protective antibodies from previous vaccinations — including against chickenpox and tetanus — remained intact.

Safety Profile and Limitations

The safety data was encouraging. Only mild-to-moderate cytokine release syndrome (CRS) occurred, manageable with standard protocols. No cases of immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) or other serious adverse events were reported. Infections were rare.

However, responses varied: not all patients achieved complete remission, and one patient experienced a disease flare after an initial medication-free period, requiring glucocorticoid treatment. Five of six patients remained immunosuppressive-free at the data cutoff of 24 to 36 weeks.

What This Means for Patients

Rheumatoid arthritis affects an estimated 18 million people worldwide. Current treatments — including biologics, JAK inhibitors and conventional DMARDs — manage symptoms but do not cure the disease, requiring lifelong medication with significant side effects. For the roughly 30% of patients who fail multiple treatments, options are particularly limited.

The Indian diaspora has a notable interest in autoimmune disease research, given that rheumatoid arthritis prevalence in South Asia ranges from 0.5% to 0.75% of the population, with women disproportionately affected.

Looking Ahead

A second phase of the COMPARE trial is now recruiting 10 additional patients. This phase will directly compare CAR T-cell therapy against an approved B-cell-targeting drug to determine whether CAR T cells deliver a stronger, longer-lasting effect and can truly reset immune memory.

If confirmed in larger trials, the approach could transform treatment for patients with severe, treatment-refractory rheumatoid arthritis — shifting the goal from lifelong symptom suppression to potential cure through a single treatment.
